title: Worker and firm heterogeneity can explain much of the variation in wage markdowns
source_unit: NBER Working Paper 35640, a model of labor supply elasticities, heterogeneous workers and firms, wage setting, and tax progressivity
geography: Conceptual model calibrated and discussed in relation to U.S. labor-market evidence; no single administrative sample is the observation unit

denominator.unit: theoretical and quantitative model; no single worker or firm sample denominator

heterogeneity_share.unit: percent of the variable component of labor-supply elasticities attributed to worker heterogeneity in the model

markdown_difference_share.unit: percent of markdown differences between large and small firms attributed to worker heterogeneity in the model

progressivity_effect.value: higher tax progressivity makes labor supply less elastic, widening markdowns and weakening the tax base in the model

policy_welfare_effect.value: the model's optimal tax progressivity is about one-third lower and associated welfare gains about two-thirds lower when these channels are included

observations.method: The authors extend a labor-market model with discrete choice over firms, production complementarities, strategic interaction, heterogeneous workers and granular firms, and compare wage-setting and tax-policy implications.
observations.uncertainty: The source is a working-paper model, not a direct estimate of any worker's wage, employer power, tax burden, or welfare. The reported shares and policy comparisons are model-dependent and should not be narrated as population prevalence or causal administrative estimates.
observations.subgroup: Modeled workers and firms differing in labor-supply elasticities, productivity, complementarities, size, and sorting; large- versus small-firm comparisons are model outputs.
observations.counterinterpretation: Worker sorting can reflect preferences, amenities, family constraints, discrimination, information, or firm quality rather than employer power alone. A model-implied markdown is not the same as observed wage theft, reduced job quality, or lack of worker voice.

boundary: This record adds a firm-worker heterogeneity mechanism: market power and policy incidence depend on who sorts into which firms and how elastic labor supply is across margins. It does not establish observed worker harm, wage markdowns for a named firm, or a universal tax-policy effect.
